nameStory: The Dark-veined Longhorn Bee gets its name from the prominent dark veins that streak through its wings like tiny roads on a map. The 'longhorn' part refers to the males' impressively long antennae that can be nearly as long as their entire body, giving them a distinctly whiskered appearance that's hard to miss.
description: Dark-veined Longhorn Bees are medium-sized, fuzzy native bees that look somewhat like small, slender bumble bees. They have robust, hairy bodies typically colored in shades of brown to golden-brown, with the females being noticeably stockier than the more slender males. These solitary bees are about half an inch long and are excellent pollinators, often seen visiting late-summer flowers with their characteristic quick, darting flight pattern.

idTips.label: Wing veins
idTips.description: Look for distinctive dark brown to black veins running through clear wings - they're much more prominent and darker than in most other bees, creating a network pattern that's visible even from a few feet away

idTips.label: Male antennae
idTips.description: Males have remarkably long, thread-like antennae that extend well beyond their head and curve gracefully - if you see a bee that looks like it's wearing long whiskers, it's likely a male longhorn bee

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Dense, soft-looking fur covers the body, feeling almost velvet-like if you could touch it - this fuzzy coat is typically golden-brown to tawny colored and helps distinguish them from the shinier, less hairy sweat bees

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Quick, darting movements between flowers with brief hovering moments - they move more erratically than the steady, direct flight of honey bees

idTips.label: Size comparison
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than bumble bees but larger than tiny sweat bees - about the size of your pinky nail from tip to first joint

habitat: Dark-veined Longhorn Bees prefer open, sunny areas with sandy or well-drained soil where females can excavate their ground nests. You'll find them in meadows, old fields, prairie remnants, and along woodland edges throughout New England. They're particularly common in areas with abundant late-season wildflowers like asters, goldenrod, and sunflowers.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not active in spring - they're still developing underground in their nest cells from the previous year's eggs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs from mid-July through early September when adults emerge to mate and forage. Look for males hovering around flowering plants and females busily collecting pollen.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall as females finish provisioning their nests with pollen balls for next year's offspring. By October, adults begin to die off as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - the next generation overwinters as developing larvae in underground nest cells, waiting for warm weather to complete their development.

funFact: Male Dark-veined Longhorn Bees are such dedicated flower visitors that they often sleep by literally biting onto flower stems with their jaws and hanging there all night like tiny, fuzzy ornaments swaying in the breeze!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other longhorn bees in the Melissodes genus, but the Dark-veined Longhorn's wing veins are notably darker and more prominent than its relatives. Remember: if the wing veins jump out at you as distinctly dark against clear wings, you're likely looking at trinodis.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'longhorn bees,' these insects are not related to longhorn beetles at all - the name simply refers to the males' extended antennae. They're also sometimes mistakenly called 'digger bees' because females excavate ground nests, but true digger bees belong to a different family entirely.
compareHints: Among its Melissodes relatives, the Dark-veined Longhorn Bee stands out for having the most conspicuous dark wing veins - while Common Longhorn Bees and Two-spotted Longhorn Bees have similar body shapes and fuzzy appearance, their wing veins are typically lighter and less noticeable. The Pickerelweed Longhorn Bee is often found near wetlands with its preferred host plant, while Dark-veined prefers drier, more open habitats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the nine other Melissodes species in New England, the Two-spotted Longhorn Bee is distinguished primarily by those diagnostic pale spots.
Among its Melissodes relatives, Drury's Long-horned Bee is distinguished by its rustic brown coloration and preference for a wide variety of late-season flowers.

Eastern Thistle Longhorn Bees are best distinguished from their Melissodes cousins by their timing and flower preferences - they're active later in summer than most relatives and show a strong preference for thistle flowers.
Among its longhorn bee relatives, the Denticulate Longhorn Bee is most reliably distinguished by its strong association with ironweed flowers rather than physical features alone.
